newsitem.title: USA: PR firm, trade groups win rulings in Florida Medicaid suit.
newsitem.headline: PR firm, trade groups win rulings in Florida Medicaid suit.

text.p: The judge in Florida's anti-tobacco lawsuit on Tuesday gave some legal shelter to two trade groups and a leading U.S. public relations firm which last represented cigarette makers in the 1960s.

Palm Beach County Circuit Judge Harold Cohen dismissed racketeering charges against Hill & Knowlton, saying the publicity agency's actions took place too long ago for it to be considered a partner in the conspiracy to misinform the public alleged by Florida in its $1 billion lawsuit.
The judge pointed out that Florida's racketeering statute being used against tobacco companies was not passed until 1977, nine years after Hill and Knowlton dropped its tobacco clients.

But the judge kept Hill & Knowlton, a unit of London-based WPP Group Plc, in the case so that if he wishes to enjoin tobacco companies or the public relations firm from continuing in the alleged conspiracy, he will have the power to do so.

Cohen also ruled during hearings before the Aug. 4 trial that neither the Council for Tobacco Research-USA Inc. nor the Tobacco Institute Inc. would be liable for paying any part of the health-care costs claimed by the state of Florida.
Neither trade group was liable because they did not manufacture or distribute cigarettes, Cohen said.

But Cohen refused to dismiss the trade groups from racketeering counts they also face. Florida says the trade groups conspired to hide the dangers of smoking through false advertising and false statements to journalists and Congress.
Both trade groups were formed in the 1950s.

The Washington-based Tobacco Institute spoke on behalf of the tobacco industry in the decades-long debate over smoking, while the research body funded medical and scientific investigations of tobacco use. Florida claims both deceived the public.

Florida is one of 40 states suing cigarette makers over the public health costs of treating sick smokers. The lawsuits helped bring about the sweeping settlement agreement announced last month in which cigarette makers agreed to pay $368.5 million over 25 years.

Florida Attorney General Robert Butterworth, who attended Tuesday's pretrial hearing, told Reuters the state is determined to go ahead with its lawsuit in spite of the agreement, which still must be approved by Congress.
"We want what's in the complaint or there is no settlement," he said.
Florida is seeking $1 billion in actual damages, which could be tripled if the state can prove the tobacco companies engaged in criminal conduct in the sale and marketing of cigarettes.
